WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: underfill alarm on FL-101, most commonly caused by a worn fill-valve seal (SOP, knowledge graph) or a blocked nozzle if no drip is observed.
- Evidence: SOP lists "Worn fill valve seal" as primary cause; prior shift log shows underfill linked to leaking valves; NCR-2026-012 confirms seals are a recurring fault.
- Difference vs history: This is the first underfill alarm recorded since the 10 Sept 2026 events; no prior leak or pressure issue noted for today.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line must be stopped for diagnosis; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour including LOTO, seal-kit change (if needed), sanitation rinse and first-bottle check (SOP, knowledge graph).
- Safety risk: LOW (no immediate hazard, but LOTO required for safe inspection).
- Financial impact: loss of one hour of production plus potential reject of underfilled bottles; exact cost not quantified in data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- MEDIUM - underfill alarm is a fault that stops the line and requires LOTO, but only a single alarm has occurred (no three-alarm systemic trigger, no safety event).

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action (follow SOP & knowledge-graph steps):
Step 1: Safety - Press the normal STOP button (do NOT use emergency stop). Put the machine in LOTO as per SAF-003 (lock isolator, tag with name/date, verify lockout). Wear required PPE (safety shoes, cut-resistant gloves, safety glasses, hearing protection).
Step 2: Diagnosis - Open the checkweigher report to identify the under-filling valve number(s).
Step 3: Inspection - Visually inspect the identified valve(s):
   - If a valve is dripping, this indicates a worn seal. Call maintenance to replace the seal kit (WI-FL101-001) - do NOT increase fill time.
   - If no drip is seen, lock out the machine (already in LOTO) and clean the nozzle of the identified valve (SOP step 4).
Step 4: Additional check - Verify product-supply pressure (SOP Section 12.4). If pressure is low, investigate upstream supply.
Step 5: Do NOT increase the fill-time setting (factory set 3.2 s, SOP Section 10). Changing it is prohibited and was the cause of NCR-2026-012.
Step 6: If three or more underfill alarms occur in this shift, stop production, raise a maintenance work order, and notify the maintenance supervisor (SOP step 6).

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Replace any worn fill-valve seals identified during inspection using WI-FL101-001 (15 min per valve, 30-45 min for 1-4 valves). Follow mandatory sanitation rinse and first-bottle check before restart.

Preventive action:
- Adhere to the seal-kit replacement interval (every 3 months or 1 500 running hours, whichever is first) as per work instruction.
- Monitor checkweigher reject rate hourly; if >1 bottle/100 over an hour, alert shift lead (knowledge-graph early warning).
- Enforce the "no fill-time change" rule; any deviation must be approved by engineering.
- Keep a minimum stock of 10 SEAL-FV-24 kits in the spares cabinet (knowledge-graph).

Who to notify:
- Maintenance Supervisor (for seal replacement or persistent underfill)
- Shift Lead (to record alarm and any production impact)
- Quality Lead (if product rejects exceed limits)

SOURCE DATA:
- FL‑101‑SOP.txt Rev 1.0 (Sections 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 8.1, 10, 11, 12.1, 12.4) – specification & procedure
- FL‑101‑Work‑Instruction.txt – seal‑kit wear guidance (no timestamp)
- FL‑101‑NCR.txt (NCR‑2026‑012, closed 18 Jan 2026) – past seal replacement & fill‑time rule
- DemoBottling‑Shift‑Log‑2026‑09‑10‑Night.csv (underfill alarms 01:30, 03:20, 04:45) – prior event pattern
- Knowledge‑Graph entry for FL‑101 (verified) – fault definition, causes, correct response, specifications
- WI‑FL101‑001 (seal‑kit replacement steps) – referenced in SOP & knowledge graph (no timestamp)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: underfill alarm on FL‑101, most commonly caused by a worn fill‑valve seal (SOP, knowledge graph) or a blocked nozzle if no drip is observed.
- Evidence: SOP lists “Worn fill valve seal” as primary cause; prior shift log shows underfill linked to leaking valves; NCR‑2026‑012 confirms seals are a recurring fault.
- Difference vs history: This is the first underfill alarm recorded since the 10 Sept 2026 events; no prior leak or pressure issue noted for today.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: line must be stopped for diagnosis; estimated downtime ≈ 1 hour including LOTO, seal‑kit change (if needed), sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check (SOP, knowledge graph).
- Safety risk: LOW (no immediate hazard, but LOTO required for safe inspection).
- Financial impact: loss of one hour of production plus potential reject of underfilled bottles; exact cost not quantified in data.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- MEDIUM – underfill alarm is a fault that stops the line and requires LOTO, but only a single alarm has occurred (no three‑alarm systemic trigger, no safety event).

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
Immediate action (follow SOP & knowledge‑graph steps):
Step 1: Safety – Press the normal STOP button (do NOT use emergency stop). Put the machine in LOTO as per SAF‑003 (lock isolator, tag with name/date, verify lockout). Wear required PPE (safety shoes, cut‑resistant gloves, safety glasses, hearing protection).
Step 2: Diagnosis – Open the checkweigher report to identify the under‑filling valve number(s).
Step 3: Inspection – Visually inspect the identified valve(s):
   - If a valve is dripping, this indicates a worn seal. Call maintenance to replace the seal kit (WI‑FL101‑001) – do NOT increase fill time.
   - If no drip is seen, lock out the machine (already in LOTO) and clean the nozzle of the identified valve (SOP step 4).
Step 4: Additional check – Verify product‑supply pressure (SOP Section 12.4). If pressure is low, investigate upstream supply.
Step 5: Do NOT increase the fill‑time setting (factory set 3.2 s, SOP Section 10). Changing it is prohibited and was the cause of NCR‑2026‑012.
Step 6: If three or more underfill alarms occur in this shift, stop production, raise a maintenance work order, and notify the maintenance supervisor (SOP step 6).

Root cause fix (permanent solution):
- Replace any worn fill‑valve seals identified during inspection using WI‑FL101‑001 (15 min per valve, 30‑45 min for 1‑4 valves). Follow mandatory sanitation rinse and first‑bottle check before restart.

Preventive action:
- Adhere to the seal‑kit replacement interval (every 3 months or 1 500 running hours, whichever is first) as per work instruction.
- Monitor checkweigher reject rate hourly; if >1 bottle/100 over an hour, alert shift lead (knowledge‑graph early warning).
- Enforce the “no fill‑time change” rule; any deviation must be approved by engineering.
- Keep a minimum stock of 10 SEAL‑FV‑24 kits in the spares cabinet (knowledge‑graph).

Who to notify:
- Maintenance Supervisor (for seal replacement or persistent underfill)
- Shift Lead (to record alarm and any production impact)
- Quality Lead (if product rejects exceed limits)

WHAT IS THE ISSUE:
- Root cause: Infeed jam caused by obstruction (likely a chipped or damaged bottle) at the star wheel, compounded by possible guide-rail mis-alignment - evidence from SOP "Infeed Jam" causes list and high-confidence alarm log of prior jam with chipped bottle (2026-09-07) and current description of bottles stuck near the star wheel.
- Difference vs historical pattern: Prior jam occurred after a 330 ml bottle changeover and a chipped bottle was identified; the current incident reports no recent changeover and no chipped bottle noted, suggesting the jam may be due solely to an unexpected bottle obstruction rather than a changeover error.

WHAT IS THE IMPACT:
- Production impact: Line stopped (FL-101 infeed jam alarm) - line down until jam cleared.
- Safety risk: HIGH (requires LOTO, reaching into machine, potential for broken glass).
- Financial impact: Not quantified in source data; line downtime implies loss of production capacity.

HOW CRITICAL IS IT:
- HIGH
- Justification: Jam requires LOTO and production stop; safety rules mandate lockout before any jam clearing; recurring jam type (infeed jam) has occurred previously, meeting HIGH minimum.

HOW TO ADDRESS IT:
- Immediate action:
  Step 1: Safety - Press STOP, then perform LOTO per SAF-003 (switch off power at main isolator, apply personal lock, tag with name/date, verify machine cannot start).
  Step 2: Diagnosis - Wear cut-resistant gloves; open guard doors; inspect the star wheel and infeed for jammed bottles and any chipped or damaged bottles.
  Step 3: Fix - Remove jammed bottles manually; if any bottles are chipped or broken, discard them; check guide-rail position against the bottle size (refer to Changeover sheet CS-FL101) and lock rails in correct position; ensure the matching star wheel is fitted.
  Step 4: Verify - Remove LOTO, restart machine at 60 bottles per minute for 2 minutes, observe feed for any further blockage, then return to normal speed (120 bpm). Confirm no further alarms.
  Step 5: Quality - Quarantine any bottles removed that show damage; inspect first 20 bottles after restart for fill quality.
- Root cause fix (permanent solution): After any bottle-size changeover, always verify guide-rail position and lock; implement a pre-start visual inspection of the infeed for foreign objects; adjust feed conveyor speed if jams recur.
- Preventive action: Add a checklist item to the shift start-up sheet to confirm guide-rail lock and clear infeed; train operators to report any chipped bottles immediately; schedule periodic cleaning of the star wheel area.
- Who to notify: Maintenance Supervisor, Shift Lead, Quality Lead.
